rationale: Start with a broad scouting gradient at mid temperature to elute all 10 compounds if possible and map the overall retention window. This gives a first view of early/late peaks and whether truncation, excessive compression, or unretained compounds are likely.

All compounds eluted cleanly and fairly early, so trim the gradient window to the observed elution region to reduce wasted high-organic range and improve time while keeping peaks inside the gradient. This should test whether a narrower, better-targeted window preserves resolution and raises CRF.

The broad window was clearly better; now test a steeper version to trade some resolution for a shorter run and see whether the critical mid-cluster pair is slope-sensitive. Comparing this directly against injection 1 isolates the effect of tG.

The 10 min gradient is faster but over-compresses the critical 5–7 cluster, while 20 min fully resolves it; an intermediate slope should recover enough resolution there with only a modest time penalty. This directly brackets the optimum between injections 1 and 3.

The optimum is likely very close to the current 14–20 min range, with the limiting pair strongly slope-sensitive. A 16 min gradient should give a bit more separation for the 6/7 pair than 14 min while likely keeping the run short enough to preserve a near-maximal CRF.

Since 14 min is best so far and 16 min is already slightly penalized by time, the optimum likely lies just below 14 min if the critical pair can stay acceptable. Testing 12 min completes the local slope scan and should show whether a slightly faster gradient can beat the current CRF.

The critical 6/7 pair is strongly slope-sensitive and may also benefit from a modest temperature shift without changing the favorable 14 min timing. Since 14 min is near-optimal in time, probe selectivity at lower temperature to see if that pair opens enough to improve the resolution term toward 1.0.

Lowering temperature worsened selectivity by collapsing a different pair, so test the opposite direction at the currently optimal 14 min slope. A modest increase to 45 C may shift the critical cluster favorably while keeping the run similarly short.

Temperature shifts hurt selectivity, so stay at 40 C and refine slope on the slower side of the optimum. With 16 min already nearly fully resolved but slightly time-penalized, 18 min tests whether the scoring maximum coincides with the point where the resolution term just reaches 1.0.

The last peak is far separated from the main cluster, so a slightly lower phi1 may better focus the useful gradient range without pushing anything too late. This tests whether a modestly narrower high-organic limit can improve the critical mid-cluster spacing at the same near-optimal run time.

The slight reduction of phi1 improved CRF, suggesting the useful gradient window is narrower than 0.05–0.95. Step phi1 down once more to see if the critical 6/7 pair opens further without incurring a time penalty from pushing the last peak too late.

The 0.05–0.90 window is the best selectivity region so far, and the remaining question is whether a slightly steeper version can keep the critical pair acceptable while shortening the run further. This checks whether the optimum shifts to shorter tG once the gradient window is better focused.

At the improved 0.05–0.90 window, 14 min is excellent but the critical pair still limits the resolution term slightly. A 16 min gradient should test whether that pair reaches full resolution in this window with only a small enough time penalty to possibly exceed the current best.

The 0.05–0.90, 14 min method is near-optimal, so only a selectivity tweak might still improve it. A larger downward temperature step is worth one targeted test because small temperature changes reshuffled the critical cluster, and 30 C could separate the limiting pair differently than 35 or 45 C.

The first peak is still comfortably retained at the best method, so slightly raising phi0 may concentrate the gradient effort on the crowded middle region without sacrificing the early peaks. This tests whether narrowing the low-organic end improves the limiting 6/7 spacing while preserving the favorable 0.90 upper bound.

The best method so far came from shifting phi0 upward, so now pair that with a slightly narrower upper bound to further center the gradient on the crowded elution region. This may gain a bit more selectivity for the limiting mid-cluster pair while likely keeping the run within the no-penalty time zone.

A perfect CRF has been reached, so this run is only to probe whether the optimum is part of a broader plateau or if further tightening the low-organic end hurts early retention. Raising phi0 one more step while keeping the successful upper bound and slope tests the robustness of the optimum without changing too many variables.

Two neighboring methods give perfect CRF, so map the upper edge of this optimum plateau by increasing phi0 once more. This checks whether the first peak is becoming effectively unretained and whether the no-penalty perfect region extends to an even shorter practical method.

The perfect region includes phi0 0.15 and phi1 0.85, so test whether trimming the upper end one more step keeps all peaks in the sweet spot and preserves full score. This explores whether the optimum plateau extends toward an even tighter gradient window around the crowded cluster.

The plateau seems centered around phi0 0.10–0.15 and phi1 0.80–0.85, so this fills the remaining corner of that local optimum region. It checks whether the slightly lower phi0 with the tighter upper bound can also deliver a perfect score or define the boundary more clearly.

The perfect region is clearly around phi0 0.10–0.15 and phi1 0.85, so test the opposite upper-side corner to define the plateau boundary. This checks whether the extra high-organic range still preserves a full score when paired with the stronger low-end focus at phi0 0.15.

A full score has already been achieved, so use the remaining injections to probe the local boundary in gradient slope around one of the optimal windows. Shortening tG at phi0 0.10, phi1 0.85 tests whether this optimum is robust to a faster method or if 14 min is the clear minimum for perfect resolution.

Since both 0.10/0.85/14 and 0.15/0.85/14 are optimal, test the faster 12 min gradient at the other optimal window corner. This defines whether either member of the perfect plateau tolerates a shorter tG better, while staying close to the proven best region.

The remaining unknown in the optimal window is the slower-side slope boundary: 12 min is too steep, while 14 min is perfect. Testing 16 min at one optimal composition confirms how broad the perfect plateau is in tG and whether full resolution persists with a modest extra time cost.

Use the final run to symmetrically complete the slower-side boundary test at the other perfect optimum. This confirms whether both CRF=1.000 methods share the same narrow optimum in tG, while keeping the experiment centered on the proven best region.
